asr.expected: Here's the first surprise. We found at least five different proposals under this label — black-hole universe, or BHU for short. A closed universe inside a black hole. A collapse that bounces instead of crushing to a point. A universe that inherits its parent's spin. Universes that reproduce, tuning the numbers built into physics. And baby universes with entirely different fingerprints. Five ideas — and no shared prediction. We wrote what we found into a closing record — the document this video reports from.

asr.expected: To test an idea, the model has to risk being wrong. It needs a number, a range, or a distinctive pattern that a measurement can miss. And if you find it, it has to point back at that one idea — not at three different ones. In the whole family we surveyed, the closing record found one clean numerical test. It uses neutron stars—the ultra-dense collapsed cores of exploded stars. The ones we can time as they spin are called pulsars, and their mass can be measured.

asr.expected: One proposal — called cosmological natural selection — says universes have children: every black hole buds off a new universe with slightly different physics. Over many generations, that would tune physics toward making black holes. In the Brown–Lee–Rho chain our record surveyed, the Brown–Bethe maximum neutron-star mass is about one and a half times the mass of our Sun—one point five solar masses. Their paper says a neutron star at approximately two solar masses or above would put that chain in ‘serious doubt or simply falsify’ it. That's a real test — a number that could be proven wrong.
